claims.text: The initial material is a crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticle composed of five or more metals.
Adding a small amount of tungsten or molybdenum can overcome structural or chemical instability in these nanoparticles at 773–1173 K.
Tungsten and molybdenum are refractory metals.
Introducing an additional refractory-metal constituent increases the configurational entropy of mixing.
Increasing configurational entropy stabilizes disordered solid-solution phases relative to ordered intermetallic phases.
Configurational-entropy stabilization reduces structural or chemical instability in refractory-metal-modified nanoparticles.
Refractory-metal-modified nanoparticles will exhibit better stability and degradation resistance than otherwise identical unmodified nanoparticles.
The predicted stability improvement applies throughout the 773–1173 K catalytic regime.
Solid-solution formation in multicomponent alloys depends on factors including atomic-size difference and enthalpy of mixing.
Particle size and shape may affect the amount of refractory metal required for stability.
Thermal exposure combined with in-situ X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and energy-dispersive spectroscopy can be used to compare modified and unmodified nanoparticles.
Failure to observe improved stability or degradation resistance in the modified nanoparticles would falsify the hypothesis.
